Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Kentucky statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Kentucky property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A taxpayer appealing a PVA real property assessment must first request a conference with the property valuation administrator or deputy, held before or during the inspection period. (KRS 133.120(1)(a) Appeal procedure; source)
  • A taxpayer still aggrieved after the PVA conference may appeal to the county board of assessment appeals by written petition to the county clerk stating reasons, identifying the property and stating the taxpayer's opinion of fair cash value. (KRS 133.120(2)(a)-(b); source)
  • The appeal must be filed no later than one workday after the inspection period ends (KRS 133.045); the Department of Revenue may extend conference and filing deadlines by up to 25 days. (KRS 133.120(2)(c)-(d); source)
  • The board of assessment appeals holds a public hearing for each taxpayer appeal and fixes the assessment at fair cash value. (KRS 133.120(3)(a); source)
  • A person aggrieved by the board's decision may appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals under KRS 49.220; a taxpayer who skipped the county board or failed to appear cannot appeal directly to the Board of Tax Appeals. (KRS 133.120; source)
  • Assessment standard is fair cash value; PVAs commonly use sales comparison for homes. All real property is subject to revaluation every year and each parcel must be physically inspected at least once every four years. (The Assessment Process for Real Property | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Kentucky sells certificates of delinquency (tax liens) to third-party purchasers, not the property itself; county clerks run sales from mid-July through late October. (Delinquent Property Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Counties must advertise each sale and list the certificates in the local newspaper and on the clerk's website at least 30 days before the sale. (Delinquent Property Tax | Department of Revenue; source)

  1. Find out what the closing attorney needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in Kentucky.

What a cash sale of a Kentucky house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Kentucky.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Kentucky disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Kentucky

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Kentucky change, so confirm details with the official office or a Kentucky attorney or tax professional.

Kentucky offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • DOR set the maximum homestead exemption at $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 tax periods. (DOR Sets 2025-2026 Homestead Exemption; source)
  • To qualify, a person must be at least 65 during the tax period or classified as totally disabled; the application goes to the local PVA no later than December 31 of the eligible tax year. (DOR Sets 2025-2026 Homestead Exemption; source)
  • The applicant must own and maintain the property as a personal residence; only one exemption per residential unit is allowed. (KRS 132.810(2); source)
  • The exemption amount is adjusted every two years if the cost-of-living index has changed by at least 1%. (KRS 132.810; source)
  • When title to exempted property is transferred, the owner, executor, trustee or agent must report the transfer to the PVA; the exemption is tied to the owner, not the property, and a new owner must apply if eligible. (KRS 132.810(3)(h); The Assessment Process for Real Property; source)
  • Disabled applicants under 65 generally reapply annually, except service-connected totally disabled veterans and individuals found totally and permanently disabled under Social Security or other Kentucky statutory rules. (KRS 132.810; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Kentucky statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

This guide covers what official sources say about Kentucky estate and inheritance tax. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • There is no Kentucky estate tax; Kentucky has an inheritance tax on the beneficiary's right to receive property. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Class A beneficiaries (surviving spouse, parent, child, grandchild, sibling and, under the 2026 amendment, nieces and nephews) are exempt from inheritance tax; the 2026 amendment applies to decedents dying on or after January 1, 2026. (KRS 140.070 (2026 Ky. Acts ch. 198); source)
  • Class B (e.g., daughter-in-law, son-in-law, aunt, uncle, great-grandchild) is taxed at 4% to 16%; Class C (all others) at 6% to 16%. (KRS 140.070; source)
  • Class B beneficiaries get a $1,000 exemption and Class C a $500 exemption. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • A return is due within 18 months of death; a 5% discount applies if paid within nine months, and tax over $5,000 may be paid in 10 annual installments. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • If all taxable assets pass to exempt beneficiaries and no federal Form 706 is required, an Affidavit of Exemption suffices for closing the estate. (Inheritance Tax | Department of Revenue; source)

Kentucky Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero closing costs

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Kentucky statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Kentucky evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act where adopted, for unpaid rent the landlord may terminate if rent is not paid within seven days after written notice. (KRS 383.660(2); source)
  • For other material noncompliance, the landlord may give written notice that the lease will terminate not less than 14 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied within 15 days. (KRS 383.660(1); source)
  • A landlord may not recover possession by self-help, including cutting off heat, electric, water or other essential services. (KRS 383.690; source)
  • Eviction is by forcible detainer complaint to District Court; the warrant issues to the sheriff and trial is by the court unless a party demands a jury. (KRS 383.210; source)
  • A landlord who conveys premises with a dwelling unit subject to a rental agreement in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for events after written notice to the tenant of the conveyance. (KRS 383.600(1); source)
  • A landlord may not retake possession by self-help or by interrupting essential services. (KRS 383.690; source)

A Kentucky deed is recorded with the county office named in the sources below. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Transfers between parent and child or grandparent and grandchild for nominal consideration are exempt from the transfer tax. (KRS 142.050(7)(l); source)
